catalog_quote: IV. EL ACENTO. El acento prosódico de la palabra recae generalmente en la penúltima sílaba. V. CANTIDAD VOCALICA. Hay un fenómeno en las variedades del quechua del centro del Perú que demanda mucha atención de los que quieren aprender a entender y hablar el quechua. [...] Se refiere al hecho de que hay dos clases de vocales en cuanto a su cantidad, cortas o largas. [...] 1. Se halla una vocal larga solamente en una sílaba abierta, es decir, en una sílaba que empieza con una consonante y termina con una vocal. [...] 2. Para identificar una vocal larga hay que escuchar el ritmo de la palabra. Todas las sílabas tienen la misma duración excepto la de vocal larga y que por ser más larga también suena un poquito más fuerte. [...] 5. Otro fenómeno que tiene que ver con la cantidad vocálica es el hecho de que la primera persona se señala mediante la prolongación de la vocal. Cuando es sujeto se alarga la última vocal del verbo y cuando es posesivo se alarga la última vocal del sustantivo. Ejemplos: aywaruu yo fui / wamraa mi niña
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: IV. STRESS. The prosodic stress of the word falls generally on the penultimate syllable. [...] V. VOWEL QUANTITY [...] 2. To identify a long vowel one must listen to the rhythm of the word. All syllables have the same duration except the long-vowel syllable, which, being longer, also sounds a little stronger. [...] 5. Another phenomenon related to vowel quantity is that first person is marked by lengthening the vowel: as subject, the last vowel of the verb is lengthened; as possessor, the last vowel of the noun.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (403-page scan-only scan of the SIL file, no text) and rendered PDF page 21 = book p. 22 to an image. The page reads exactly: "IV. EL ACENTO / El acento prosódico de la palabra recae generalmente en la penúltima sílaba." followed by "V. CANTIDAD VOCALICA" and, as item 2, "Para identificar una vocal larga hay que escuchar el ritmo de la palabra. Todas las sílabas tienen la misma duración excepto la de vocal larga y que por ser más larga también suena un poquito más fuerte." Item 5 (book pp. 23-24, PDF 22-23, from the scanned file we hold) reads "Otro fenómeno que tiene que ver con la cantidad vocálica es el hecho de que la primera persona se señala mediante la prolongación de la vocal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is generally on the penultimate syllable. Long vowels (which in this variety occur only in open syllables and mark, among other things, first person by lengthening the word-final vowel) are said to sound somewhat stronger, so a word-final long vowel may carry perceptible prominence; the source hedges with 'generalmente' but names no specific exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated explicitly ('generalmente'). The remark that long-vowel syllables sound 'a little stronger', together with word-final 1st-person vowel length, is the likely exception class; Cerrón-Palomino 1987: 124-125 (comparative, second-hand for this lect) reports final-syllable accent on such Junín forms ([wasí:] 'my house').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('acento prosódico de la palabra'); citation forms in a pedagogical grammar; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1990 Lecciones describe the variety of south-east Pasco (Huachón, Paucartambo, Ninacaca, Huayllay) and the provinces of Junín and Tarma (preface, p. 5), which SIL tags as North Junín Quechua [qvn] = nort2980; Adelaar 1977 (the named-but-unreachable grammar) describes the Tarma-town dialect of the same language (WALS 'Quechua (Tarma)' qta -> nort2980). Cerrón-Palomino's 'juninense' remarks are about central (Junín) Quechua I generally and include Huanca (huay1241/jauj1238), so they are not a first-hand statement for nort2980.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. (34) aywa-mu-ra-ygi ~ aywa-mu-ra-y go-H-PA-2S 'You came.' In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme referring to first-person subject or possessor is immediately followed by a word boundary
new_statements.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. & Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, ch. 3.2 (Quechua phonology)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Saved file holds the 13 archive.us.archive.org response for item languagesofandes0000adel, 1 hit each) and the chained passage. I re-ran the API myself (check_fts/): c1 'In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as', c2 'In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyl- labic word form', c6 'In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme' reproduce q1/q3/q6 exactly, so the compiler quote is the scanned text of the book; the only differences are the joined line-break hyphens ('polysyl- labic', 'delimita- tion' -> 'polysyllabic', 'delimitation') and the truncation before the pa…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate) and as Black, Bolli & Ticsi 1990 p. 22 ('recae generalmente en la penúltima sílaba'); adds the two mechanisms behind the exceptions (elided final syllable; word-final first-person -VV) with a Tarma example, and states that non-first-person final length is neutralised so penult stress holds. Compatible with Cerrón-Palomino 1987 pp. 124-125 (Junín final-syllable accent on first-person length forms) already held by the project in this directory.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (the family-wide default, which Adelaar & Muysken apply to Tarma / northern Junín). Word-final stress arises in Tarma and northern Junín when a final syllable is elided (aywa-mu-ra-ygi ~ aywa-mu-ra-y 'you came'), and, as in all Quechua I dialects, when the first-person long-vowel morpheme (-: subject/possessor) stands word-finally; other word-final length is neutralised and stress then falls on the penult as usual. Interjections and emphatic expressions may also carry final stress (alalaw).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) interjections/emphatic expressions with final stress (alalaw 'how cold!'); (2) Tarma and northern Junín: final stress after elision of a final syllable; (3) Quechua I generally: stress stays on a word-final first-person long vowel (wayi 'house' vs wayi-: 'my house' per the q13 snippet). The book's other non-penultimate systems (Pacaraos phonemic final/penult; Ancash and Cajatambo initial/weight-sensitive; Chachapoyas initial) concern other dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken refer to 'Tarma and the dialect of northern Junín' (quantity-insensitive Yaru group; Adelaar's 1977 Tarma Quechua fieldwork base), which is the variety Glottolog files as nort2980 / ISO qvn North Junín Quechua (the catalog's 'Quechua del sureste de Pasco y el norte de Junín'). The first sentence of the quoted passage is family-wide ('most Quechua dialects'); the first-person-length sentence is for Quechua I as a whole; only the elision sentence and example (34) are specific to Tarma / northern Junín. The book was read through archive.org full-text-search snippets (controlled-lending copy; refused could not be reached by automated download), chained at their overlaps, not from a page scan.
